Article Title: US welcomes removal of International Criminal Court chief prosecutor Karim Khan
Article Text:
Why Khan was removed



US steps up campaign against ICC



The International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday voted to remove its chief prosecutor, Karim Khan, over findings of "serious misconduct and serious breach of duty", nearly two years after allegations of sexual misconduct first surfaced.The decision comes as the Hague-based court faces mounting pressure from the United States, which has intensified its campaign against the institution.The ICC's 125 member states approved Khan's removal by a large majority during a meeting of the Assembly of States Parties, the court's governing body. Khan, a British barrister, has consistently denied the allegations against him.The move was welcomed by the United States, which has recently escalated its criticism of the ICC. Last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced what he described as a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to US sovereignty."The 56-year-old prosecutor was accused of sexual misconduct involving a female aide. According to documents reviewed by The Associated Press, Khan allegedly engaged in a sexual relationship with the staff member and later attempted to prevent her from pursuing the allegations.Khan has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.Announcing the decision, the Assembly of States Parties said Khan was removed for "serious misconduct and serious breach of duty."Human Rights Watch welcomed the decision, saying the court must maintain the highest standards of accountability."The ICC should hold itself to the highest standards. This includes ensuring a safe workplace with effective and credible mechanisms available to staff or others who experience abuse, including sexual violence or harassment," Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch told AP.Khan's legal team criticised the proceedings, arguing that he was not given a fair opportunity to defend himself before member states voted.Attorney Tayab Ali said Khan's "removal was determined by a process in which he was never given a fair opportunity to be heard, and in defiance of the conclusions of the independent judges who examined the full evidential record."He added that Khan's lawyers would challenge the decision "through all available legal mechanisms." The Assembly will now begin the process of electing a new chief prosecutor.Khan's removal comes as the Trump administration intensifies its confrontation with the ICC. In a statement issued last week, secretary of state Marco Rubio said Washington would pressure countries to withdraw from the court, sanction organisations working with it and impose travel bans on ICC officials."The United States was launching a 'sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to US sovereignty,'" Rubio said.The Trump administration has already imposed sanctions on 13 ICC officials, including Khan, after the court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over the war in Gaza. The ICC has also investigated alleged crimes involving US personnel in Afghanistan.
Article Summary: Karim Khan was accused of sexual misconduct involving a female aide. The move was welcomed by the United States, which has recently escalated its criticism of the ICC. Khan's legal team criticised the proceedings, arguing that he was not given a fair opportunity to defend himself before member states voted.

Article Title: Girl died after gene-editing treatment in China: Report
Article Text:
The girl, given the pseudonym “Mei,” died a week after receiving a spinal infusion of trillions of viruses

(This is an AFP story)

WASHINGTON: A six-year-old Chinese girl died last year after receiving an experimental gene-therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition, according to an investigation by Science and Retraction Watch.The girl, given the pseudonym "Mei," died a week after receiving a spinal infusion of trillions of viruses last March designed to penetrate the brain and fix a rare genetic condition that caused her mild cognitive impairment, the report said Thursday. But her parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks, the report said.The lead researcher went on to publish a paper on related animal studies in journal, Nature, that made no mention of Mei, noting only "bridging the gap between preclinical research and clinical translation remains a significant challenge."Mei had a rare genetic condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, known to affect just 237 people worldwide. Caused by a single mutated DNA base, a T that should be a C, most affected individuals have a normal life expectancy, have larger-than-normal heads and intellectual deficits, though the extent varies widely.The trial was led by neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, one of several researchers globally racing to turn base editors -- a more precise form of the CRISPR gene editor -- into custom treatments for children with rare genetic conditions.Seven experts who reviewed the details said Qiu and his team downplayed the risks and went ahead despite low odds of success. They also called for a full review of the data submitted for the Nature paper, saying some findings could warrant a retraction. The case also raises questions about whether such treatments should be initially tested on patients with non-fatal conditions.
Article Summary: A six-year-old Chinese girl died last year after receiving an experimental gene- therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition. The girl, given the pseudonym "Mei," died a week after receiving a spinal infusion of trillions of viruses last March. Her parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks.

Article Title: Burnham brings a 'No. 10' to Manchester to kickstart English 'devolution'
Article Text:
​British PM Andy Burnham formally opened his newly created northern office​

LONDON: British PM Andy Burnham formally opened his newly created northern office on Friday, promising "a different way of running Britain" as he bids to reverse decades of centralising power over England in London.Unveiling No 10 North in the northwestern city of Manchester, Burnham -- who replaced Keir Starmer as premier on Monday -- pledged power would "flow" away from London's Whitehall governing district to spur economic growth. "It's not just a new office," he told staff at the city centre site. "This is the place where Whitehall meets the rest of the country."The former Greater Manchester mayor says the thriving city-region - which has outscored Britain's national performance in various areas, including economic growth - provides a model for other parts of the country. He aims to work from No 10 North at least once a week, dismissing criticism it was a "short-lived gimmick". "It creates that sense of a more balanced country and that big things can be done from here," Burnham insisted.Devolution experts, however, appear unconvinced. 'De-concentration' is "something done in even very centralised states and in itself doesn't signify any transfer of power", academic and policy adviser Alan Trench told AFP."At most, it transfers public sector jobs and the lives and incomes of those who hold them."The UK - comprising England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland - saw significant constitutional reforms in the late 1990s that created devolved parliaments in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast. London also obtained a directly elected mayor and a scrutinising assembly. But England itself remains one of Europe's most centralised nations despite the creation of some regional mayors and other bodies in the last decade, experts say. "Nowhere in England has any devolved law-making power," Trench noted.University of Glasgow professor Nicola McEwen said English devolution had been "very asymmetric", hindered by London largely viewing it as something that "happens somewhere else".Burnham experienced the limits of the current system during his nine years as Manchester mayor. Now in London, he has ordered departments including the finance ministry to make "targeted transfers of overarching strategic functions" to No 10 North, a minister told parliament this week.McEwen said handing No 10 North a strategic role was "positive" but success would still hinge on Whitehall agreeing to cooperate. However, University of Aberdeen politics professor Michael Keating noted it was "deeply ironic that to deal with centralisation you set up a central govt department that's going to decide exactly who gets what". Under "real" devolution "you get out of their way", he said.Others noted relocating civil servants was neither bold nor original. Around 80,000 govt staff already work in northwest England, Burnham's spokesman acknowledged this week. Burnham, who met the nationalist leaders of Scotland and Wales on Thursday, has said little about further devolution -- other than ruling out supporting independence referendums.(This is an AFP story)
Article Summary: British PM Andy Burnham formally opened his newly created northern office on Friday. Burnham pledges to reverse decades of centralising power over England in London. He aims to work from No 10 North at least once a week, dismissing criticism it was a "short-lived gimmick"

Article Title: Pakistan, Iran explore fresh talks with US in China-initiated push: Report
Article Text:
Damage in Iran

(This is a Reuters story)

ISLAMABAD: Pakistan is exploring a path towards a resumption of stalled US-Iran talks over ending their nearly five-month-old war, three Pakistani sources said, following a push initiated by China. Exploratory discussions took place during a visit by Iran's interior minister Eskandar Momeni to Islamabad this week - his second within the last 10 days, the sources said. Momeni, who is considered close to Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps, met Pakistani govt members and army chief Asim Munir, according to Pakistani govt statements. All three sources cautioned that the obstacles to any talks with the US remain high.Pakistan has found itself in an increasingly complicated situation as a potential future mediator. Earlier this week, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, a close ally of Islamabad that signed a mutual defence treaty with Pakistan last year. Pakistan relies on Saudi financial support, and Islamabad has firmly condemned recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Being seen as too receptive to Iranian arguments could risk frustrating Riyadh.But Islamabad is similarly dependent on Beijing, which has also been a key financial backer of Islamabad, and which has economic interests in finding a diplomatic solution to reopening key West Asian trade routes. Pakistan's foreign minister, Ishaq Dar, also discussed the new effort with Chinese officials when he visited China last week, all three Pakistani sources said."The Chinese are unhappy because Iran's attacks on other Gulf states and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz are hitting their interests," a Pakistani govt official said. In a statement, China's foreign ministry said "China supports the mediation efforts made by Pakistan and other parties."Beijing is Iran's largest trading partner and primary buyer of its crude oil despite international sanctions on Tehran. Over the years, China has also increased support for Iran's security through dual-use components, chip equipment and satellite navigation systems, even though China has not overtly provided military aid to Iran since the war began.
Article Summary: Pakistan has found itself in an increasingly complicated situation as a potential future mediator. Being seen as too receptive to Iranian arguments could risk frustrating Riyadh. Islamabad is similarly dependent on Beijing, which has also been a key financial backer of Islamabad, and which has economic interests in finding a diplomatic solution.

Article Title: 10 killed, nearly 100 injured in Russian strike on Ukraine defence event
Article Text:
Addressing the nation, Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the attack.

At least 10 people were killed and nearly 100 injured after a Russian ballistic missile struck a defence industry event in Ukraine's Kyiv region on Friday, prompting President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to criticise the decision to hold such a gathering during wartime.Ukraine's Emergency Services said rescue operations at the site, located north of the capital, had been completed. Images released by the agency showed emergency workers searching through piles of rubble near several residential houses.Addressing the nation, Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the attack but also questioned the decision to organise a defence-related exhibition while the war continues."Of course, the cause of this attack is Russian missiles, nothing but Russian terror," he said, according to news agency Reuters."However, we have said a thousand times that under these wartime conditions, with such an enemy, it is absolutely unacceptable to hold any weapons exhibitions with large crowds of people, especially near residential buildings."The event, organised by a drone manufacturers' association, was being held a short distance from the outskirts of Kyiv. A spokesperson for Ukraine's General Staff said the venue did not fall under the military's jurisdiction, but stressed that any such event should have been conducted with "maximum security measures".Kyiv regional acting governor Ruslan Oliynyk announced that Saturday would be observed as a day of mourning following the strike.The Ukrainian Council of Defence Industry confirmed that representatives of the country's defence sector were present when the missile hit, but said it had not organised the event.Valerii Borovyk, founder of Ukrainian drone company First Contact, told local media that the missile struck a training ground where the exhibition was taking place.Ukraine's Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said a criminal investigation had been launched to examine whether officials failed in their duties while organising and conducting the event.Russia also carried out attacks in several other parts of Ukraine on Friday. In the eastern city of Sloviansk, a Russian aerial bomb killed five people and injured nine, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin. He later said another evening strike on the city injured 16 more people and damaged residential buildings.In the northern Sumy region, a Russian drone attack killed two people, regional governor Oleh Hryhorov said.Meanwhile, in the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia, a Russian strike set a shopping centre on fire and injured several people.Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly accused each other of targeting civilians since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, although both sides deny deliberately attacking civilian populations.
Article Summary: At least 10 people killed and nearly 100 injured after a Russian ballistic missile struck a defence industry event in Ukraine's Kyiv region on Friday. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the attack but also questioned the decision to organise a defence-related exhibition.

Article Title: 'Found lying in pool of blood': Indian man found dead in Jerusalem apartment; Israeli held
Article Text:
Indian man found dead in Jerusalem (Credit/X)

An Indian national was found dead inside an apartment in Jerusalem 's Katamon neighbourhood on Thursday, with Israeli police arresting a 31-year-old man on suspicion of murder.The 40-year-old victim was "found lying on the floor with blood" around him, and authorities said the case is being investigated as a suspected criminal offence. His identity has not yet been disclosed."Following the earlier report regarding a 40-year-old foreign national from India who was found dead in an apartment in the Katamon neighbourhood of Jerusalem, officers from the Moria Police Station arrived quickly at the scene and launched an initial investigation together with forensic investigators," the Israel Police Spokesperson's Unit said, according to PTI."The preliminary investigation at the scene indicates that the incident is suspected to be criminal in nature," the police added.Police said they quickly identified and arrested a 31-year-old resident of Eilat on suspicion of involvement in the murder. The suspect, whose identity has not been released, is in custody and is being questioned.According to The Times of Israel, the victim was found lying on the floor inside the apartment with blood around him. Israeli news outlet Ynetnews reported that investigators suspect the killing has a criminal background.Jerusalem District Commander Avshalom Peled visited the crime scene and held a review meeting with senior officers. Following the initial assessment, he directed that the investigation be handed over to the Jerusalem District Central Unit (YAMAR).In a video released by the police, Chief Superintendent Yuval Reuven, commander of the Moria Police Station, described the discovery."In the Jerusalem District, at the Moriah Station, an incident was reported involving a person found in a house, covered in a significant amount of blood."He said officers immediately secured the scene and launched an investigation."Police officers arrived at the scene, cordoned off the area, and began initial investigative operations. During the investigation, a suspect for the murder was located." Reuven added that investigators moved swiftly to detain the suspect."The investigation led to the swift arrest of the suspected individual involved in the murder. Currently, additional investigative operations are underway to determine the truth about the incident."The motive behind the killing remains unclear, and police said the investigation is ongoing.
Article Summary: An Indian national was found dead inside an apartment in Jerusalem's Katamon neighbourhood. The 40-year-old victim was "found lying on the floor with blood" around him. Authorities said the case is being investigated as a suspected criminal offence. Police said they quickly identified and arrested a 31-year old resident of Eilat on suspicion of involvement in the murder.

Article Title: Russian missile strike kills six in Kyiv region as Ukraine targets Russia's biggest online retailer
Article Text:
Ukraine targets Russia's biggest e-commerce company



Ukraine says facilities supported Russian military



Small businesses bear the brunt



NEW DELHI: At least six people were killed and dozens injured after a Russian missile strike hit Ukraine's Kyiv region on Friday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, as explosions were reported in the capital during another wave of Russian attacks."Efforts to determine exactly what happened and the fate of those affected are ongoing," Zelenskyy said on Telegram.Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said multiple explosions were heard in the capital as Ukrainian air defence systems responded to the Russian assault. He urged residents to remain in shelters while air defence units worked to repel the attack.The latest strike came as Ukraine intensified its long-range drone campaign inside Russia, targeting warehouses belonging to Wildberries, the country's largest online marketplace.Ukrainian drones have struck multiple Wildberries logistics facilities over the past week, including warehouses near Moscow, in southern Russia and in Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014. According to reports, nine people have been killed and dozens injured in the attacks.The strikes are part of Kyiv's strategy to disrupt Russia's war effort by targeting logistics infrastructure and increasing the economic costs of the conflict inside Russia.Wildberries, founded in 2004 by former teacher Tatyana Kim, has grown into Russia's largest online retailer, accounting for about 52% of all online orders in the country. The platform serves between 500,000 and 800,000 sellers and operates more than 200 logistics facilities across Russia and neighbouring countries.While Zelenskyy did not mention Wildberries by name, Ukrainian authorities have said the targeted facilities were involved in supplying equipment and technical components to the Russian military.The Kremlin denied the allegation. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Kyiv was attacking civilian infrastructure.An Associated Press review of Wildberries' website found products that could be used for both civilian and military purposes, including body armour, helmets, radios and electronic equipment. Some products were labelled as "tested in the SVO" or "SVO fighters' choice," using Russia's term for its military campaign in Ukraine.The warehouse attacks have dealt a heavy blow to thousands of small businesses that rely on Wildberries to store and distribute their goods across Russia.Many sellers have taken to social media claiming that inventory stored in the damaged warehouses was destroyed. Wildberries has announced measures including reduced storage fees, free transfer of goods to other facilities and discounted loans through Wildberries Bank.The company also began compensating some affected sellers, particularly smaller businesses whose stock was damaged at its Elektrostal warehouse.Sergei Semko, a leading analyst at Moscow-based Data Insight, estimated that the attacked warehouses account for about 12% of Wildberries' storage capacity. He said losses from destroyed inventory could reach as much as $3 billion.
Article Summary: Ukrainian drones have struck multiple Wildberries logistics facilities over the past week, including warehouses near Moscow, in southern Russia and in Crimea. Wildberries has announced measures including reduced storage fees, free transfer of goods to other facilities and discounted loans through Wildberries Bank.

Article Title: NYC Upper West Side stabbing: Zohran Mamdani reveals disturbing details of 'hateful' attack
Article Text:
Zohran Mamdani

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday said police are investigating two stabbings on Manhattan's Upper West Side as possible hate crimes after witnesses and victims reported that the suspect shouted "Allahu Akbar" during both attacks.The mayor said the New York Police Department (NYPD) responded quickly and arrested 51-year-old, Raul Morales in connection with both the incidents.In a statement posted on X, Mamdani said he had been briefed on the attacks and confirmed that both victims were in stable condition."I have been briefed on today's horrifying stabbings on the Upper West Side, where an Asian man and a Jewish man were attacked. According to witness and victim statements, the perpetrator yelled 'Allahu Akbar' during both attacks. I am relieved that both victims are in stable condition," he wrote on X."The NYPD responded immediately and arrested Raul Morales in connection with both assaults, and I am grateful to the officers for their swift response," Mamdani said.He added that investigators believe mental health may have been a factor and are also examining whether the attacks qualify as hate crimes."The NYPD's initial investigation suggests that mental health may have been a factor.They are also evaluating these stabbings as potential hate crimes," the NYC Mayor said."These hateful and despicable attacks have no place in our city," he added.According to the NYPD, Morales allegedly stabbed an Asian man and a Jewish man in two separate attacks that took place about two blocks apart in broad daylight. Witnesses told police the suspect shouted the Arabic phrase "Allahu Akbar" during both assaults.Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said investigators are still working to determine a motive. She said there is no known connection between the suspect and the victims, and the initial investigation indicates that mental health may have played a role.Both victims were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries and are expected to recover. Morales remained in police custody on Thursday evening. It was not immediately clear whether he had legal representation, AP reported.Governor Kathy Hochul also condemned the attacks, saying New York stands with its Jewish and Asian communities. "Asian New Yorkers, like Jewish New Yorkers, have endured waves of hate-fuelled violence in recent years. Hate rarely stops with one group. New York will continue confronting it wherever it appears," she wrote on X.Police said the investigation is ongoing. More details awaited.
Article Summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani said police are investigating two stabbings on Manhattan's Upper West Side as possible hate crimes. The mayor said the New York Police Department (NYPD) responded quickly and arrested 51-year-old, Raul Morales in connection with both the incidents.

Article Title: Donald Trump returns to White House Correspondents' dinner months after shooting forced postponement
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump attends the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner

US President Donald Trump on Friday attended the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) dinner, nearly three months after the annual event was postponed following a shooting outside the original venue.The US president is set to address journalists from major news organisations after months of clashes with the media over coverage and press access.Ahead of the event, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said Trump's remarks would be "a combination of unifying yet vicious, and serious yet hilarious, all at the same time."The annual black-tie dinner, which celebrates press freedom and raises money for journalism scholarships, was postponed from April after a gunman attempted to breach a security checkpoint and opened fire outside the venue room at Washington Hilton, where Trump and members of his Cabinet were present.Friday's event is now being held at the Waldorf Astoria hotel under heightened security.Meanwhile, the suspect in the shooting, Cole Allen, later pleaded not guilty to charges including attempting to assassinate the president.The White House Correspondents' Association said the programme would include recognition of Secret Service officer Victor Gonzales, who was wounded while stopping the attacker, as well as Washington Hilton staff who assisted guests during the incident.Trump's appearance comes amid continued criticism from press freedom advocates over his administration's lawsuits against media organisations, restrictions on some journalists' access and other actions affecting the press. The White House has defended those measures, saying they are intended to improve accountability, protect sensitive information and address media bias.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump attended the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) dinner. The annual black-tie dinner was postponed from April after a gunman attempted to breach a security checkpoint and opened fire outside the venue room at Washington Hilton. The event is now being held at the Waldorf Astoria hotel under heightened security.

Article Title: 'White, male, Christian' report drives Trump's disclaimer push at US history museum
Article Text:
A person views displays at the Smithsonian museum a day after Independence Day celebrations (AP)

US President Donald Trump has directed his administration to install disclaimer signs outside the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, arguing that some of its exhibits present an inaccurate account of the country's past. The move is the latest step in his effort to reshape how American history is presented and comes after the White House released a report criticising the museum's portrayal of the nation's heritage.The order follows a report published by Trump's Domestic Policy Council on July 4, which claimed that the Smithsonian and the National Museum of American History fail to present history in a manner that is "inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic."The 162-page report also alleged that the institution does not adequately acknowledge the "constructive role of Christian belief" in shaping the United States. It further claimed that "White, male, and Christian Americans are regularly denigrated as the alleged embodiment of oppressive power structures."Since the Smithsonian operates independently of the executive branch, Trump cannot directly remove its leadership or rewrite museum exhibits.Instead, his executive order focuses on the public space outside the museum, where the National Park Service manages the pavements.Under the order, visitors will see signs informing them that some exhibits contain information the White House considers inaccurate. The signs will also direct people to government-approved resources offering what the administration describes as a more accurate account of American history. The order further proposes a temporary exhibition aimed at correcting what Trump believes are historical inaccuracies.The Smithsonian did not immediately respond to the latest executive order.Earlier this week, National Museum of American History director Anthea M. Hartig rejected the White House's criticism while appearing before lawmakers."As we continue to fact check the report, we unwaveringly attest that it does not fairly or accurately characterise the full body of work at the museum," she said."There is always room for improvement. But I also know the beauty and the inspiration and the expertise that lies in our collections, our exhibits, and our programming."The Smithsonian is overseen by a Board of Regents, with museum directors reporting to Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch rather than the White House.Trump's latest action forms part of a wider campaign to reshape major cultural institutions that he believes promote ideological narratives. In March, he signed an executive order targeting federal funding for programmes that advanced what he described as "divisive narratives" and "improper ideology."His administration has also pursued changes beyond the Smithsonian. Earlier this year, Trump dismissed National Portrait Gallery director Kim Sajet, calling her "a highly partisan person." He has also sought changes to historical displays at other heritage sites, including exhibits related to slavery at George Washington's former residence in Philadelphia.Critics, including historians and advocacy groups, have argued that these efforts risk downplaying difficult chapters of American history in favour of a more celebratory national narrative.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has directed his administration to install disclaimer signs outside the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. The move is the latest step in his effort to reshape how American history is presented. Comes after the White House released a report criticising the museum's portrayal of the nation's heritage.

Article Title: Trump confirms Netanyahu's US visit next week amid regional tensions
Article Text:
Trump's remark came in his speech at the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner on Friday.

United States President Donald Trump said that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will visit the US next week as the American forces continue to pound parts of Iran after peace talks fizzled out despite weeks of talks and signing of the MoU between Washington and Tehran.Trump's remark came in his speech at the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner on Friday.Netanyahu and Trump agreed to meet in the United States a few weeks ago following a phone conversation. During the call, Netanyahu congratulated Trump on the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States and praised the close relationship between the two countries.It comes as the US-Israeli war with Iran has again escalated following a breakdown earlier this month of a ceasefire reached as part of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed by the US and Iran.Israel had opposed the agreement from the outset, while its continuing military operations in Lebanon repeatedly threatened diplomatic efforts in the region.The Trump administration has also been mediating separate talks between Israel and Lebanon aimed at ending hostilities. The negotiations do not involve Hezbollah.Both sides have accepted a proposal under which Israeli-held areas in southern Lebanon would eventually be handed over to the Lebanese military.However, there has been little visible progress on the ground since March.During a meeting with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun earlier this week, Trump did not indicate when Israeli forces would withdraw from the occupied areas.Meanwhile, the US military said its Central Command had completed a 13th straight night of strikes against targets in Iran.Iran has continued to respond with attacks on US military assets across the region. Last week, a strike on a US base in Jordan killed three American soldiers.The United States has also increased its military deployment in Israel, a move that some analysts believe could signal preparations for a wider regional escalation.Netanyahu's visit will also take place as Israel's military campaign in Gaza continues. Despite a US-backed ceasefire announced last October, Israeli forces have continued issuing evacuation orders and carrying out frequent strikes across the territory.
Article Summary: Netanyahu and Trump agreed to meet in the United States a few weeks ago following a phone conversation. It comes as the US-Israeli war with Iran has again escalated following a breakdown earlier this month of a ceasefire reached as part of a Memorandum of Understanding.

Article Title: Government withdraws subpoenas of 3 reporters for The New York Times after admitting legal errors
Article Text:
David McCraw, right, general counsel for the New York Times, and Douglas Zolkind, center, attorney for the New York Times, leave Manhattan federal court

NEW YORK: Criticized by a federal judge for sloppy legal work, the government on Thursday grudgingly withdrew subpoenas that would have compelled three New York Times reporters to testify about their sources for articles about President Donald Trump 's Qatari-gifted Air Force One jet.The withdrawals in US District Court followed a remarkable back-and-forth between a visibly irritated Judge Arun Subramanian and government lawyers. They come at a time when the Trump administration is vigorously going after news organizations whose reporting and coverage it doesn't like - and also trying to crack down on leaks inside the government.The government's turnabout in the face of vigorous legal opposition and a stern reprimand from a judge marked the latest instance of the Justice Department making aggressive moves to compel journalists to identify their sources before a grand jury - only to later retreat. The administration recently withdrew similar subpoenas that sought to compel testimony from journalists for The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal related to separate national security coverage.Subramanian said he otherwise would have granted the newspaper's request to reject the subpoenas because regulations pertaining to subpoenas served on journalists maintain that they should be issued as a last resort in an investigation."Subpoenas are the last step, not the first step, but the last step," the judge said, citing rules set to protect against violations of the First Amendment. He said the government's actions had turned the law and the regulations "on its head.""When you see something like this, if this were a civil proceeding, what I would normally do is ask the parties to show causes why sanctions should not be issued," the judge said, referencing punishment for lawyers for egregious actions.After the hearing, the Justice Department lashed out at Subramanian in a statement, saying he "threatened our attorneys with sanctions unless subpoenas were withdrawn, and blocked us from presenting the meticulous process of this investigation.""The grand jury has a right to hear testimony from all material witnesses in a federal criminal investigation. This judge's conduct overrides clear longstanding principles and common sense - blocking the grand jury from receiving core evidence in a national security investigation," the statement said."Make no mistake," it added, "this investigation remains ongoing, and we will pursue justice against those threatening national security by leaking classified information, a serious federal crime."Government attorneys upbraided by judge Subramanian noted that with protections for journalists at stake, the government was required to ensure it could not obtain what it needed from any other sources before issuing subpoenas to journalists.A Justice Department lawyer, Sean Buckley, cast the government's missteps as inadvertent errors and said: "No one was trying to pull a fast one." Buckley apologized for other subpoenas that sought records for phone numbers belonging to one reporter's mother and two of the journalists' spouses."That was an error, judge, which we own," Buckley said. "It was a consequence of trying to move quickly.""These things are starting to pile up," Subramanian said, becoming increasingly testy.The hearing was held publicly despite efforts by the Trump administration to keep secret the litigation spawned by subpoenas it served on the Times' journalists to try to get them to divulge their sources.The newspaper's lawyers had challenged the validity of the grand jury subpoenas, along with subpoenas issued for phone records of several Times journalists and some of their relatives. Senior Times officials, including the paper's managing editor and general counsel, sat in the gallery watching during Thursday's proceedings.The request for phone records raised questions about the extent of the investigation being carried out by the Justice Department.David McCraw, the Times' chief newsroom lawyer, said after the hearing in a statement that it "was an important affirmation of our country's commitment to a free press.""We are pleased that the government finally conceded that the subpoenas violated the law, but they should never have been issued in the first place," he said. "We will not be deterred in the face of tactics like these."Court action comes after reporting on new Air Force One jet The new jet in question, a present from Qatar that Trump's administration spent $400 million to retrofit and upgrade, recently entered service. But Trump used an older model Air Force One jet to leave a NATO summit in Turkey earlier this month.The Times, citing anonymous sources, reported that the switch had come at the urging of the Secret Service and that the newer plane lacked some of the advanced security features of the older Air Force One aircraft, including antimissile capabilities. On social media, Trump rejected claims of security concerns.The Times wrote in a letter to the judge several days ago that two subpoenas seek records beginning on Jan. 1, long before the newspaper published articles on July 8 and July 9 that became the basis for the grand jury subpoenas.It said that lengthy stretch of records sought would indicate that the purpose of the subpoenas might have been "to forage for information about the Journalists' source relationships more broadly."The Times argued for the phone records subpoenas to be disallowed on the grounds that the government had acted in "bad faith" and ignored its own protocols by not giving the journalists advance notice that records were being sought and by demanding the information "without first conducting any serious investigation."The Justice Department has justified the grand jury subpoenas by saying that "reporters are not the targets, those leaking classified information are." The department also said it had complied with its own regulations in issuing the subpoenas and had taken "certain" investigative steps before seeking them. It said it was authorized to delay disclosure of the phone records subpoenas but decided to alert the journalists' lawyers "so that counsel could advance any arguments-regardless of merit-in furtherance of their motion. "In fighting the subpoenas, the Times' lawyers highlighted how the government's carelessness could have exposed sensitive information that had nothing to do with the journalists. The mother whose phone records were mistakenly sought is a mental health professional with confidential client relationships and one of the two spouses is the general counsel of a law firm, the lawyers said.At Thursday's hearing, a final rebuke from the judge to the government came when he asked its lawyers to assure him that it won't repeat a scenario that left one journalist being served a subpoena by an FBI agent while he was home watching the family-friendly movie "The Sheep Detectives," about sheep on a quest to solve the murder of their shepherd.Said the judge, to loud courtroom laughter: "I can't think of anything more inconsistent with 'Sheep Detective' than an FBI agent showing up at your door."
Article Summary: The government's turnabout in the face of vigorous legal opposition and a stern reprimand from a judge marked the latest instance of the Justice Department making aggressive moves to compel journalists to identify their sources. The administration recently withdrew similar subpoenas that sought to compel testimony from journalists for The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal related to separate national security coverage.

Trump said that he does not believe China or Russia are “participating” in the ongoing Iran conflict,

Article Title: America is committing trillions to rebuild. AI must help people build it
Article Text:
AI is useful, but only when it is grounded in the judgment of people

I have spent more than two decades building AI systems, and I am also a father of two young children. These two facts shape how I think about the future we are building. When AI companies claim they are building systems to replace people, I believe them. I know what this powerful technology can do, but as a parent, I worry about what we choose to do with it.The United States is entering a period of reindustrialization. Roughly $2 trillion is flowing into manufacturing, infrastructure, energy, semiconductors, and the industries that will define the future. But the people needed to build it are in short supply.What we build with AI, and who benefits from it, is still our choice. The numbers make the stakes plain. Manufacturing alone could face 2.1 million unfilled jobs by 2030, a shortage that could cost the U.S. economy up to $1 trillion that year. The construction and skilled trades sector is short more than 530,000 workers in 2026 alone. Aviation faces a projected shortage of 60,000 maintenance technicians by 2029 if the pipeline does not improve. And even as AI displaces some work in other sectors, 170 million new roles are projected to be created by 2030, roles that will require exactly the kind of skilled, experienced people we are struggling to find.The challenge isn’t simply finding more workers. It is helping people across the workforce build, share, and keep improving the know-how this moment demands. We do not have a shortage of know-how in this country, but every retirement takes decades of hard-earned know-how with it. For every five skilled workers who retire, only two enter the trades. That is the gap we should be asking AI to close.So, the question is not whether AI changes work. It will.The real question is whether we use AI to replace know-how or multiply it.Know-how earned from decades of work is different from written information. It is what people learn after years of doing real work: what to notice, when to slow down, when to escalate, when something feels off, and how to solve a problem that does not look like the textbook or the checklist.Think about a 22-year-old aviation safety mechanic on the first day of the job. Then comes a vibration, a temperature change, something that does not match what the manuals describe. An experienced mechanic may have seen that pattern before. They know when to slow down, when to escalate, and how to diagnose the problem.This need for experienced, embodied knowledge repeats across industries. An electrician wiring a new manufacturing plant. The construction supervisor who spots a problem before it becomes an accident. The manufacturing engineer who knows why a production line keeps failing. A nurse who notices a patient declining before the chart makes it obvious. The physician whose judgment helps treat complex cases. The small business owner who spent decades earning trust, training people, and learning how to serve a community.When that hard-earned know-how walks out the door, we all lose.Ford learned this the hard way. After three years of quality problems, the company turned back to about 350 veteran engineers and technical specialists to mentor younger workers, lead design reviews, and improve the AI tools used to catch defects earlier. Ford’s lesson was clear: AI is useful, but only when it is grounded in the judgment of people who know the work. Their expertise was not the cost to cut. It was the competitive advantage Ford could not afford to lose.Ford is not alone. Research shows that more than a third of companies that conducted AI-driven layoffs had to rehire more than half the workers they let go.Too much of today’s AI is designed to keep people coming back for answers, not to help them build lasting know-how. That is the same mistake social media made: engagement over agency. AI should not become another technology that takes human agency away. It should help people become more capable, not more dependent.What we need is AI that works alongside experienced people, continually learning from the decisions they make and the problems they solve, and helps bring the next person up to speed faster. In some roles, that could compress expertise that once took years to build into weeks or months of guided learning.That is one reason we started Cognisee: to build AI that learns with how people think, judge, and act, and puts that hard-earned judgment within reach of every person who comes after them, so we never have to choose between experience and scale.Building takes more than capital. It takes people who know how to build, fix, operate, and improve the systems our country depends on. And it takes making sure their know-how multiplies, not disappears.The promised age of abundance cannot be built by leaving people behind.The true measure of AI is not how much work it takes away from people. It is how much value it helps us create for families, businesses, communities, and nations.Because the future will not be built by AI alone. It will be built by people whose knowledge, judgment, and purpose are multiplied by it.
Article Summary: Manufacturing alone could face 2.1 million unfilled jobs by 2030, a shortage that could cost the U.S. economy up to $1 trillion that year. We do not have a shortage of know-how in this country, but every retirement takes decades of hard-earned know- how with it. For every five skilled workers who retire, only two enter the trades. That is the gap we should be asking AI to close.

Article Title: SpaceX launches 13th Starship test flight, deploys 20 next-generation Starlink satellites
Article Text:
SpaceX's Starship rocket lifts off for a test flight from Starbase, Texas

SpaceX on Friday launched its Starship rocket on its 13th test flight, sending the world's largest and most powerful launch vehicle into space carrying 20 next-generation Starlink satellites as the company advanced its plans for future Moon and Mars missions.The 407-foot (124-metre) rocket lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility in southern Texas after an earlier launch attempt was aborted last week when six engines on the first-stage booster failed to ignite. The company replaced the engines before Friday's successful liftoff.The hour-long mission marked the second flight this year of the upgraded Starship V3. The booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico, while the spacecraft completed its planned re-entry and splashdown in the Indian Ocean after travelling more than 10,000 miles (16,000 km).During the mission, the spacecraft deployed 20 Starlink V3 satellites, which extended their solar arrays and antennas and attempted laser communications with existing Starlink satellites in orbit before eventually burning up during re-entry, as planned.SpaceX said six of the newly launched satellites carried cameras to photograph Starship's heat shield during flight. The spacecraft's heat shield also featured sensors to record the extreme conditions experienced during launch, while some thermal protection tiles were painted white to simulate damage as part of a durability test.The company is working to ensure Starship can safely survive atmospheric re-entry and eventually return to its launch site for reuse. SpaceX has already demonstrated catching the rocket's booster using giant mechanical arms and plans to use the same method for the spacecraft in future missions.Nasa is closely watching the programme as it plans to use a modified Starship as the lunar lander for the Artemis III mission, which aims to return astronauts to the Moon. The agency wants Starship to complete testing and reach orbit before astronauts begin docking practice next year.Beyond Nasa's lunar programme, SpaceX founder Elon Musk has said Starship will serve as the primary vehicle for future missions to Mars.The latest test flight had been delayed twice—first by the last-second launch abort on July 16 and then by poor weather caused by Tropical Storm Bertha.
Article Summary: SpaceX launches its Starship rocket on its 13th test flight. Rocket carried 20 next-generation Starlink satellites into space. Earlier launch attempt was aborted when six engines failed to ignite. SpaceX founder Elon Musk has said Starship will serve as the primary vehicle for future missions to Mars.

Article Title: Quote of the day by John Cena: 'By the time I was 15 and I stepped in the high school gym...' and how a bullied kid changed his life forever
Article Text:
'By the time I was 15 and I stepped in the high school gym, I was just stronger than everybody'

"By the time I was 15 and I stepped in the high school gym, I was just stronger than everybody,"

The boy in the basement

The science of personal change

Real effort in a world of shortcuts

What West Newbury teaches us

A teenager stands in front of a bathroom mirror, wearing baggy clothes for one main reason: to hide from bullies. Long before the bright stadium lights, movie success, or world championship belts, there was a small town in Massachusetts called West Newbury. There, a young boy with a unique fashion sense and haircut kept getting pushed around. The short walk to the school bus was a daily source of fear.To stop feeling weak, the boy asked his father for a bench press set. He started lifting weights in his basement at age 12, treating every workout as protection against being picked on. By the time he started high school, everything had changed. John Cena recalled years later.What sounds like a bragging comment from a famous athlete is actually a story about self-defense. Cena was not born huge. He built his body because he felt he had to. His quote points to the moment when personal hard work pays off, turning a weakness into real physical strength.When John Cena spoke about his youth in interviews, he was reflecting on growing up in West Newbury during the early 1990s. As the second of five brothers, Cena was regularly teased and pushed around by older kids in his neighborhood.He did not start lifting weights to play professional football or become a bodybuilder. He just wanted the bullying on the sidewalk to stop.He began training at home with a basic weight set, learning as he went. His commitment was total. While other kids spent their middle school years hanging out, Cena spent three years building muscle in his basement.When he finally walked into the high school weight room at 15, the kids who used to shove him on the bus noticed right away. The bullying stopped immediately. Cena did not seek revenge; his new size alone was enough to end the trouble. What started as a way to protect himself became a lifelong passion. It carried him to Springfield College, where he played NCAA Division III football as an All-American center, before leading him into professional wrestling and acting.The idea behind Cena's transformation connects to psychology, specifically the concept of an "internal locus of control" introduced by psychologist Julian B. Rotter in 1954. People with an internal focus believe their own choices shape their lives, while those with an external focus feel controlled by outside forces.For a 12-year-old dealing with bullies, the school day feels random and unfair. You cannot easily change how other kids act. The weight room, however, is a place where efforts bring clear results. If you put 100 pounds on a bar and lift it regularly, your body grows stronger. Weights do not care about social status or popularity. It is a fair test, and passing it builds honest confidence.This also matches Stoic philosophy, such as the teachings of Epictetus on focusing only on what you can control. Epictetus taught that while we cannot control other people, we have full control over our own habits. Cena picking up a barbell was an early lesson in Stoicism: he stopped trying to fix the bullies and focused on changing himself.Cena’s story matters today in a world full of quick fixes and social media filters. People can easily pretend to be successful or confident online without doing the actual work behind it.Real strength cannot be faked. Whether learning a trade, building fitness, or running a business, real progress requires long hours of quiet work. The moment Cena stepped into the high school gym was simply the public reveal of those hidden years.Think of a programmer who studies coding for years before taking on complex problems no one else can fix. Or a business owner who studies a market for months before launching a product. The principle is the same: true confidence is not a performance. It comes naturally from the work you have already finished.When Cena entered that gym at 15, he was not acting tough. He simply had three years of hard work backing him up.Cena kept his early success in perspective. In the same interview about his high school years, he noted that being the strongest kid in West Newbury was a small achievement in the real world. It meant a lot to a teenager in a small town, but it was only the first step.That grounded mindset kept him humble. The gym taught him that there is always someone stronger and a bigger challenge ahead. His goal was never to pick fights, but to make sure he was never helpless again.Strength built out of hard times creates lasting character. It forms people who do not need to start arguments because they know they can handle tough situations. The effort put in that Massachusetts basement changed Cena's path, showing that while you cannot pick where you start, you can always choose how hard you work for what comes next.
Article Summary: John Cena started lifting weights in his basement at age 12 to protect himself from bullies. Cena did not start lifting weights to play professional football or become a bodybuilder. He did not seek revenge; his new size alone was enough to end the trouble. Cena's story matters today in a world full of quick fixes and social media filters.

Article Title: Indian-American doctor speaks out after viral video sparks 'go back to India' abuse over bindi
Article Text: An Indian-American doctor has spoken out after receiving a wave of racist comments online over a video in which she wore a bindi, saying she was stunned by the level of anti-Indian abuse directed at her despite being born and raised in the United States.Dr Karishma Reddy shared her response in an Instagram video after a light-hearted post about a patient interaction unexpectedly triggered hateful remarks, with several users telling her to "go back to India".Reddy said the reaction was unlike anything she had experienced before, adding that her years working in healthcare had largely been marked by respect and acceptance."I have never seen so much anti-Indian rhetoric in my entire life," she said, explaining that the medical community had always been welcoming and that she had rarely felt like a minority in that environment.Responding to comments targeting her Hindu faith, Reddy also addressed misconceptions about the significance of cows in Hinduism. She said many Hindus avoid eating beef out of respect for the role cows historically played in sustaining families by providing milk, rather than because of simplistic stereotypes often shared online.She said she was saddened that people appeared increasingly comfortable posting hateful messages on social media and urged users to treat others with kindness."I hope that this at least opened your mind to Hinduism and cows," she said, adding, "Be kind, please."The video drew widespread support from viewers, many of whom praised Reddy for calmly addressing the abuse instead of responding with anger.One user credited the doctor with transforming their life through medical treatment, writing: "Dr Reddy saved my life when she gave me the opportunity to live without pain every day. Take the hate elsewhere."Another user commented: "So proud of you for showing up anyway. You saved me giving me my gender affirming care and I am so grateful that you exist in the healthcare space and take up space as yourself and the way you support each of your patients!"
Article Summary: Dr Karishma Reddy shared her response in an Instagram video after a light- hearted post about a patient interaction unexpectedly triggered hateful remarks. Reddy said the reaction was unlike anything she had experienced before, adding that her years working in healthcare had largely been marked by respect and acceptance. She urged users to treat others with kindness.

Article Title: Big Bear bald eagle Jackie's health update: Lead poisoning ruled out, bright and strong but critical after life-saving blood transfusion
Article Text:
Jackie was critically injured after a fight. Her partner Shadow gave her blood.

The Ojai Raptor Center said Jackie did not suffer lead poisoning, as millions have been waiting for a health update on the beloved bald eagle who is also one of the internet-famous Big Bear Valley Bald Eagles. Jackie and her mate Shadow became internet celebrities through a popular 24/7 live-stream camera maintained by the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley in California. After remaining missing for several days, Jackie was found alive but injured."Her kidney inflammation also appears to have improved, the eagle continues to perch and eat, and there is slight improvement in her energy," said Eliza Cameron of the Ojai Raptor Center.Jackie needed blood and it was her mate Spirit who donated the blood. Spirit was carefully evaluated before donating blood.Experts treating Jackie, however, confirmed that she has been suffering from anemia. "Her condition remains critical at this time, and this is not a straightforward case, so we are consulting with several specialists," Cameron said. "A treatment plan is being developed to ensure we're covering all bases while we work to determine the cause of anemia."According to available records, Jackie was believed to be the first bald eagle born in the Big Bear Valley in 2012. In 2014, Shadow was born.In 2016-17, Jackie took a nest with a mate named Mr B. Jackie and Mr. B mated, but Jackie did not lay eggs. Since she was only just five years old it is possible she was still too young to be sexually mature.In 2017-2018, Jackie laid eggs, which hatched and were named Stormy and BBB. BBB did not survive.Then Shadow came to the nest and refused to leave. Mr B eventually left the area and Jackie accepted Shadow as her new mate.The couple became an internet sensation and hatched many chicks.In 2026, Jackie was injured in a fight with other intruder eagles.
Article Summary: Jackie the bald eagle was critically injured after a fight. Her partner Shadow gave her blood. Jackie and her mate Shadow became internet celebrities through a popular 24/7 live-stream camera maintained by the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley in California. The Ojai Raptor Center said Jackie did not suffer lead poisoning.

Article Title: 8 people entered a sealed glass world believing they could survive for two years. Then the oxygen began to disappear
Article Text:
Why Biosphere 2 was built in the first place

How oxygen quietly began disappearing from the sealed atmosphere

The chemistry that explained the missing oxygen

A crew breathing air equivalent to a Himalayan peak

Why the intervention mattered for the project's scientific standing

Personal conflict overshadowed the underlying science

What happened to Biosphere 2 after the first mission ended

A troubled experiment that still shapes science today

Deep in the Arizona desert near Oracle sits one of the strangest experiments ever built, a sealed, 3.14-acre glass and steel enclosure called Biosphere 2. Constructed between 1987 and 1991 at a cost of roughly $150 million, funded largely by Texas billionaire Edward Bass, it was designed to test whether humans could live inside a fully self-sustaining artificial ecosystem, complete with its own ocean, rainforest, desert, savannah and farmland. On 26 September 1991, four men and four women, known as biospherians, sealed themselves inside for what was meant to be a two-year mission. What followed became one of the most closely watched, and ultimately most controversial, science experiments of the decade.The facility took its name from the idea that Earth itself is Biosphere 1, and this artificial version was meant to model it in miniature. According to reporting on the University of Arizona's official description of the project, the enclosure was built as a materially closed ecological system, meaning almost nothing was meant to pass between the inside and outside world except sunlight. Beyond its scientific goals, the project was also framed as an early test of the kind of closed life support systems that future space colonies on the moon or Mars might eventually require, with the crew farming their own food and recycling their own water, waste and air.Roughly three months into the mission, the crew began noticing a troubling pattern in their regular air quality tests: oxygen levels that had started at a normal 20.9 per cent were steadily falling. According to the peer-reviewed paper titled Oxygen loss in Biosphere 2 , published in Eos, Transactions American Geophysical Union, by researcher Jeffrey Severinghaus and colleagues including Wallace Broecker of Columbia University's Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory, oxygen levels dropped from 21 per cent to just 14 per cent over the first sixteen months of closure, a decline serious enough to begin causing health problems for the crew inside.The mystery deepened because the drop in oxygen did not match up with a corresponding rise in carbon dioxide, the gas normally released whenever oxygen is consumed through respiration. Severinghaus and his co-authors identified the cause: microbes in the facility's unusually rich soil were consuming oxygen at a much faster rate than expected, but crucially, the carbon dioxide they produced was reacting with calcium hydroxide in the building's exposed concrete to form calcium carbonate, a process called carbonation. This meant carbon was effectively being locked away into the walls themselves, masking the true scale of the oxygen loss and making the problem far harder to diagnose in real time.By January 1993, conditions inside had become severe enough that outside intervention was required. Mark Nelson, one of the original eight crew members, later wrote for the University of Arizona Press that the crew had been living with oxygen levels around 14 per cent, equivalent to being at roughly 15,000 feet of elevation, despite the facility itself sitting at only around 3,900 feet in southern Arizona. Nelson described the moment Mission Control finally pumped supplemental oxygen into the sealed structure, raising internal levels to 26 per cent, higher than Earth's normal atmosphere, and recalled feeling decades younger within minutes, along with hearing the sound of crew members running for the first time in many months.The need for outside oxygen fundamentally changed how the mission was judged. As a demonstration of a truly self-sustaining closed habitat, the first mission did not succeed on its own terms, since a system that requires external resupply to keep its occupants safe cannot be considered fully closed. At the same time, the episode produced a genuinely valuable scientific finding: the interaction between rich soil, microbial respiration and curing concrete had not been anticipated at the design stage, and diagnosing it added real, lasting insight into how closed ecological systems actually behave under sustained real-world conditions.Beyond the oxygen crisis, tension within the crew itself became a major part of the story. According to NPR's coverage of the project, disagreements among the eight biospherians over how the project should be managed became international headline material, often overshadowing the underlying science entirely. By the time the crew emerged in September 1993 after completing their full two-year mission, the original group had split into two factions that reportedly were no longer on speaking terms with each other, following stress from cramped shared quarters, food shortages caused by lower-than-expected crop yields, and disputes over the project's direction.A second, shorter mission began in 1994 but lasted only about six months before being cut short. Ownership of the facility subsequently changed hands several times, and Columbia University took over managing its research programme for a period in the mid to late 1990s before eventually stepping back. In 2007, the facility was donated to the University of Arizona, which continues to operate it today as an active Earth system science research centre, now employing dozens of staff, including researchers studying rainforest dynamics, ocean acidification and climate change using the same sealed biomes originally built for the Biospheres.Despite its rocky beginnings and lingering reputation as a 1990s punchline, complete with tell-all books and a Pauly Shore film loosely inspired by the project, Biosphere 2's core scientific legacy has held up in ways its early critics may not have anticipated. The facility demonstrated that life support in a closed system cannot be neatly separated into biological and mechanical components, since the ecosystem, the machinery meant to support it, and even the building materials themselves all interact in ways that are difficult to predict in advance. More than three decades later, that hard-won lesson continues to inform research into life support systems for future long-duration space missions, even as the story of the crew's two years sealed inside a shrinking supply of breathable air remains the detail most people still remember first.
